polymarket-648383.brief: The question is whether a proposition containing a one-time tax on people or households with at least $1 billion of wealth passes at the California election on 3 November 2026. On 17 June the California Secretary of State announced that initiative 25-0024A1, a one-time tax of up to 5% on taxpayers and trusts with covered assets over $1 billion, was eligible for the 3 November ballot (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2026-news-releases-and-advisories/california-secretary-state-shirley-n-weber-phd-announces-new-measure-eligible-november-2026-general-election-ballot-imposes-one, quotes checked). The qualified-measures list shows it as Proposition 40, an initiative constitutional amendment and statute, alongside competing Propositions 41 and 42 (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/qualified-ballot-measures). The Legislative Analyst's Office says Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of billionaires who were California residents on 1 January 2026, due in 2027, and that Propositions 41 or 42 could stop it from becoming law if either gets more yes votes, even if Proposition 40 has a majority (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026, quotes checked). CalMatters reports the same nullification mechanism (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/). A Citrin-POLITICO poll published 19 October found 46% of likely voters in favour and 43% opposed, about unchanged from a month earlier, with the headline saying it fell short of majority support (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/19/california-billionaire-tax-poll-01125462). Ballots began mailing on or before 5 October and no result exists yet (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/). For the base rate, Ballotpedia's inventory for 1910 to 2025 records ballot initiatives approved 36% of the time, legislatively referred measures 69%, and 57.6% of all 1,307 statewide measures (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Ballot_Measures:_Historical_Ballot_Measures_Factbook). No earlier California one-time billionaire tax exists for comparison. It is unclear whether a measure that wins a majority but is nullified by a rival measure counts as passing, which depends on how the market reads the word. The answer would change with new polling showing a majority, heavy late spending on either side, or court action on the competing measures.

facts.fact: On June 17, 2026, the California Secretary of State said initiative 25-0024A1, a one-time tax of up to 5% on taxpayers and trusts with covered assets over $1 billion, became eligible for the November 3, 2026 ballot, with certification set for June 25, 2026 unless the proponent withdrew it.

As of the Secretary of State’s qualified-measures list, Proposition 40 (“Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers”) is a qualified initiative constitutional amendment and statute on the November 3, 2026 statewide ballot, alongside competing Propositions 41 and 42.

The Legislative Analyst’s Office states Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of billionaires who were California residents on January 1, 2026, due in 2027, and that Propositions 41 or 42 could stop it from becoming law if they receive more yes votes even if Proposition 40 has a majority.

The official voter guide says county officials begin mailing ballots on or before October 5, 2026, and Election Day is November 3, 2026; as of October 20, 2026, the election has not been held and no official result exists.
CalMatters reports that if Proposition 41 or 42 receives more votes than Proposition 40, Proposition 40 would be nullified.
A Citrin-POLITICO poll published October 19, 2026 found 46% of likely voters in favor of Proposition 40 and 43% opposed, about unchanged from a month earlier.
